claims.text: As-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy films have a disordered, single-phase hexagonal structure.
The as-deposited films exhibit a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
Low-temperature post-deposition annealing promotes a moderate increase in chemical short-range order.
Enhanced short-range order homogenizes nucleation of the magnetostructural transition.
Annealing between approximately 200°C and 400°C for several hours can promote moderate ordering without secondary-phase precipitation or excessive grain growth.
Greater and more spatially uniform short-range order reduces local compositional fluctuations.
Greater and more spatially uniform short-range order reduces defect-pinning centers at the transformation-phase boundary.
Annealing-induced short-range order reduces defect-induced inhomogeneity.
Reduced defect-induced inhomogeneity alleviates pinning of magnetostructural transformation fronts.
Alleviating transformation-front pinning causes the magnetostructural transition to proceed more uniformly.
The annealed films will have a broader magnetocaloric entropy-change response than the as-deposited films.
The annealed films will exhibit less hysteresis than the as-deposited films under low-applied-field cycles.
Annealing will slightly shift the transition temperature.
Annealing may marginally reduce the peak magnetocaloric entropy change.
Annealing-induced reduction of hysteresis will improve reversibility of the magnetocaloric response.
Annealing will enhance heat-exchange performance relative to the as-deposited films.
The baseline films have high hysteresis because atomic-arrangement inhomogeneity and defects act as pinning centers.
The baseline films have limited heat-exchange properties because of atomic-arrangement inhomogeneity and defects.
Excessive annealing temperature or duration may produce secondary phases or over-ordered structures that do not follow the predicted trend.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant hysteresis reduction together with failure to observe broadening or a transition-temperature shift would falsify the proposed short-range-order mechanism.
